question: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of tremors in both hands for the past few months. He has had difficulty buttoning his shirts and holding a cup of coffee without spilling its content. He has noticed that his symptoms improve after a glass of whiskey. His maternal uncle began to develop similar symptoms around the same age. He has bronchial asthma controlled with albuterol and fluticasone. Examination shows a low-amplitude tremor bilaterally when the arms are outstretched that worsens during the finger-to-nose test. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Tremors in both hands" -> "Difficulty buttoning shirts and holding a cup of coffee" -> "Improvement of symptoms after a glass of whiskey" -> "Possible alcohol-responsive tremor" -> 70% CHAIN: "Low-amplitude tremor bilaterally" -> "Worsening during finger-to-nose test" -> "Cerebellar dysfunction" -> "Likely essential tremor" -> 80% CHAIN: "Maternal uncle with similar symptoms" -> "Possible genetic predisposition" -> 60% CHAIN: "Bronchial asthma controlled with albuterol and fluticasone" -> "No direct relevance to tremors" -> 90% CHAIN: "Alprazolam" -> "Anxiolytic, not first-line for tremors" -> 70% CHAIN: "Levodopa" -> "Used in Parkinson's disease, not first-line for essential tremor" -> 80% CHAIN: "Primidone" -> "First-line pharmacotherapy for essential tremor" -> 95% CHAIN: "Propranolol" -> "Beta-blocker, effective in essential tremor" -> 90% CHAIN: "Valproic acid" -> "Not first-line for essential tremor" -> 70%
analysis: The patient's symptoms of tremors, especially with a family history of similar symptoms, suggest a diagnosis of essential tremor. The fact that his symptoms improve after consuming alcohol is a classic feature of essential tremor. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for essential tremor is propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker.
